segments.t: Hi, I'm Alice, and welcome to T L D R Daily, your quick tour of today's tech news.
And I'm Michael. Today is heavy on remote code execution bugs, plus a few platform and A I stories that matter for how teams build and ship.
Let's start with the one that needs action first. The InfoSec newsletter says a critical flaw in Apache Roller is being exploited right now, and attackers don't need to log in.

It affects Roller versions four point zero through six point one point four. The bug is an unsafe deserialization problem in the X M L R P C endpoint, so a remote attacker can run arbitrary code. The fix is to upgrade to six point one point six or later.
Absolutely.
And if you can't patch today? There's a workaround, right?

Yes. Set enabledForExtensions to false in the web dot x m l file, remove the X M L R P C servlet mapping, and restart. But here's the catch. Turning off X M L R P C in the admin screen does not protect older versions.
Good point.
Next, the same newsletter covers seven critical fixes from the P H P Foundation. One of them, nicknamed phpAfterShell by Depthfirst, can be chained with another flaw to reach code execution.

It applies to any application running an affected P H P version with file-based sessions. So if your sessions live on disk, check your version today. Depthfirst even built a proof of concept showing the chain.
Right.
And there's a Java story too. The Dev Ops newsletter calls it Java4Shell, a critical flaw rated nine point two out of ten in OpenJDK's Base64 decoding on chips with A V X five twelve support.

It hits OpenJDK seventeen point zero point six and later on x86 sixty-four hardware. The report says it can give attackers pre-authentication code execution in tools like Jenkins, Confluence and Tomcat. The InfoSec newsletter covered it earlier this week and named Jira, Artifactory, Keycloak and Elasticsearch as well.
Wow, that's a lot.
So what do people do?
Upgrade OpenJDK, or disable the Base64 intrinsics. And do it for your build servers first, because those hold the keys to everything else.
Exactly. One more bug from that newsletter. Researchers at Veria found a one-byte heap overflow in Ruby.

It comes from how single-byte encodings turn the German sharp s into two letters, while the loop only expects one. The report says Git Hub Enterprise Server and Git Lab are among the affected software.
Fair point.
Now to data exposure. Rakuten Securities in Japan warns that customer data for about four point four seven million accounts may have leaked.

That includes annual income, financial assets, dates of birth and employers. Login I Ds and account codes may also be out for more than eleven million accounts. Totally the kind of data scammers love.
Totally.
And in London, Transport for London took its Oyster photocard website offline after attackers compromised details for about two hundred sixty-five thousand customers.
Definitely. The InfoSec newsletter says the photocard site is now offline, which tells you how serious the account compromise was.
Also in the InfoSec newsletter, Bitdefender says the EggStreme malware was rebuilt after its first disclosure, with stronger encryption and new commands that list Active Directory users and groups.

Now to A I risk. The InfoSec newsletter points to a report that Meta staff are worried about its Muse assistant. Internal chats say Muse could read Signal messages on Android through setup permissions.
What does Meta say?
Meta calls the reports of mixed-up accounts hallucinations, and says the bug is fixed. Reuters, as cited there, found the Android access was real, so the permissions question remains.
That fits the theme on the I T side. Microsoft introduced agent controls, a managed Azure service that sets and checks policies for A I agents.

It's built on the open source Agent Control Specification and Agent Hooks. It judges agent actions with safety classifiers, L L M judges, and fixed rules written in Rego. The point is runtime governance for mixed fleets of agents, without writing your own policy system.
Exactly, that's the part to watch.
The I T newsletter also says Apple will add a warning in macOS twenty-seven point three that makes people think twice before letting third-party agents control a Mac.
And the main TLDR newsletter reports that Apple is hiring for its own autonomous agent that can write code, browse and control apps.
Let's do the platform and Dev Ops picks. Microsoft's early report on last week's Microsoft three sixty-five outage says the problem slipped through because test labs used the wrong traffic mix.
Right. The linked analysis says throughput can vary by orders of magnitude depending on key skew. So load tests only count if they look like production.
Quick-fire round. Palo Alto Networks will buy Applied Compute for four point five billion dollars in stock.
Elastic's survey of more than four hundred security pros says ninety-six percent of teams use A I in the S O C, but only eighteen percent enforce governance.
Git Lab nineteen point six adds Rapid Diffs, with the first file loading in about one point five seconds.
And Postgres nineteen is out, with online table repacking and a new plan advice extension.
Anthropic stock debuted on the Nasdaq at one hundred eleven dollars fifty and closed day one at ninety-seven seventeen, according to the main newsletter.
Alright, the three actions for today. First, patch or mitigate Apache Roller, and treat it as already exploited.
Second, update P H P and OpenJDK, starting with build and identity servers.
Third, write down which A I agents have access to your data, and put policy checks in front of them.
That's our brief. Thanks for listening. I'm Michael.
And I'm Alice. See you tomorrow.
